briefs.osteoporosis:
Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment

who is screened early · T-score vs Z-score · when to treat · drug cautionsHas every risk factor been counted, and does each one point the way you assume?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Screen every woman at 65 with DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry). Run the risk-factor list before applying that default:

  • Exam shorthand (question banks): any one risk factor (prior fragility fracture, family history of hip fracture, smoking, low body weight, chronic glucocorticoids) means DEXA now; when DEXA now is an option, it is the scored answer. ⚠︎ The task force rule differs (next line).
  • USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) 2025: postmenopausal and under 65 with a risk factor such as low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking or excess alcohol (the USPSTF also lists menopausal status), use a clinical risk tool such as FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool), then DEXA if the risk is raised; no fixed threshold. Men: evidence insufficient (not a recommendation against). Androgen deprivation therapy: the exam keys DEXA ⚠︎.

Obesity protects bone; low body weight (under 58 kg) is the risk factor. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis without a scan.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria T-score – against a young adult peak; postmenopausal women and men 50 or older: -1.0 or above normal, -1.0 to -2.5 osteopenia, -2.5 or below osteoporosis · Z-score – against age- and sex-matched peers; premenopausal women, men under 50, children: -2.0 or below is below expected and needs a secondary-cause search · Clinical osteoporosis – a hip or vertebral fragility fracture, regardless of T-score
Risk factors Nonmodifiable – advanced age, postmenopausal (the entry condition for screening under 65, not a trigger by itself), low body weight, White or Asian, malabsorption, hypercortisolism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic liver or kidney disease · Modifiable – smoking, excess alcohol, inactivity, glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, proton pump inhibitors, low vitamin D or calcium, estrogen deficiency (premature menopause, oophorectomy), aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy · Family history – FRAX asks about a parental hip fracture, not a sibling's; a sibling fracture counts only in the exam shorthand
Management and treatment
Management ladder: osteoporosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Smoking cessation, calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention; always concurrent, never enough alone once a risk factor existsAge 65: DEXA. Risk factor: DEXA now (exam) or risk tool first (USPSTF) ⚠︎
2Check calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and creatinine; correct low vitamin D firstT-score -2.5 or below, hip or vertebral fragility fracture, or osteopenia with FRAX 20% major or 3% hip ⚠︎
3Bisphosphonate: upright with water, stay upright 30 minutes; drug holiday after about 5 years oral or 3 years intravenous if low riskVery high risk: an anabolic agent (teriparatide or abaloparatide)
Drug cautions Bisphosphonate – esophagitis; long-term osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture · Denosumab – rebound vertebral fractures if stopped abruptly; never simply discontinue · Romosozumab – cardiovascular boxed warning · Raloxifene – lowers breast cancer risk but raises venous thromboembolism · Height loss or kyphosis – vertebral imaging
Practice
  1. 55-year-old woman asks when to check her bones menopause at 50 body mass index 31 Never smoked; no fractures; no parental hip fracture BP 126/80 mm Hg · no glucocorticoid use → DEXA at 65 → no trigger on either list; menopause at a normal age with no risk factor waits until 65 (the USPSTF lists menopausal status; read here as the entry condition ⚠︎): DEXA at 65; obesity protects bone
  2. 56-year-old woman, postmenopausal, asks about bone screening weighs 52 kg smokes a pack a day; her mother fractured a hip No fractures of her own; no glucocorticoids BP 122/76 mm Hg · body mass index 19 → Run FRAX now → DEXA now (the exam shorthand) is not offered; of these, the USPSTF step is a clinical risk tool such as FRAX, then DEXA if risk is raised; no drug before a diagnosis
  3. 48-year-old woman has taken prednisone 10 mg daily for 4 months for sarcoidosis expects to continue for a year Still menstruating; no fractures BP 132/84 mm Hg · body mass index 26 → DEXA now, regardless of age → chronic glucocorticoids call for DEXA now, regardless of age
  4. 68-year-old woman has never had bone density testing feels well and walks daily no fractures, no falls Takes no medications; never smoked; asks whether she needs a scan BP 136/82 mm Hg · body mass index 24 → DEXA now → every woman 65 or older is screened with DEXA; a risk tool alone does not replace it
  5. 60-year-old woman has a DEXA T-score of -1.8 at the hip no fractures of her own her father fractured a hip at 78 Nonsmoker BP 128/80 mm Hg · calcium and vitamin D normal → Run FRAX → osteopenia: run FRAX and treat if the 10-year risk is 20% or more for a major fracture or 3% or more for a hip fracture
  6. 32-year-old woman has a fragility fracture of the wrist fell from standing height on a sidewalk regular periods; no glucocorticoids DEXA ordered to evaluate her bones BP 108/68 mm Hg · body mass index 18 · Z-score -2.3 → Z-score; secondary-cause workup → a premenopausal patient is read by the Z-score, and a score of -2.0 or below sends you after secondary causes: celiac disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, an eating disorder, amenorrhea (her regular periods argue against it)
  7. 57-year-old woman with a T-score of -2.7 is about to start alendronate rarely goes outdoors in winter drinks no milk No calcium or vitamin D level on file; no kidney disease BP 124/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Check vitamin D and calcium first → check calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D first: an untreated vitamin D deficiency turns a bisphosphonate into hypocalcemia
  8. 64-year-old man starts androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer no fractures, no falls no glucocorticoids Asks whether his bones need checking BP 138/84 mm Hg · body mass index 27 · testosterone castrate level → Screen with DEXA now → androgen deprivation therapy (and an aromatase inhibitor in a woman) is a specific cause of bone loss; the exam keys baseline DEXA at its start, although USPSTF finds the evidence for screening men in general insufficient ⚠︎
  9. 57-year-old woman has back pain after bending to lift a laundry basket radiograph: vertebral compression fracture no trauma No DEXA on file BP 130/80 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Start a bisphosphonate now → a vertebral or hip fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis by itself: start a bisphosphonate now
  10. 57-year-old woman who smokes asks for hormone therapy to protect her bones T-score -2.6 no hot flashes or night sweats Smokes a pack a day BP 134/86 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Decline estrogen; start alendronate → avoid estrogen: smoking adds to its venous thromboembolism risk, and hormone therapy is not first-line for bone; raloxifene also raises venous thromboembolism risk and is not first-line; a bisphosphonate treats a T-score of -2.6
  11. 70-year-old woman on alendronate for 8 years has thigh pain aching for weeks, worse with walking no fall Radiograph: cortical thickening with a transverse line in the lateral femoral shaft Afebrile · calcium normal → Atypical femoral fracture → thigh pain after years of bisphosphonate is an atypical femoral fracture: image both femurs
Transferable rule

Run the risk-factor list first and apply the age default only when it comes back empty. Check that each variable points the way you assume: obesity raises cardiovascular, endometrial and sleep apnea risk but lowers osteoporosis risk.
